Description

With all the new resolutions, here is a new functionality of CSSPseudoElement:

CSSPseudoElement has the following:

  • The type attribute is a string representing the type of the pseudo-element.
  • The element attribute is the ultimate originating element of the pseudo-element.
  • The parent attribute is the originating element of the pseudo-element (Either Element of CSSPseudoElement for nested pseudo-elements).
  • The pseudo(type) method to retrieve nested pseudo-elements.

CSSPseudoElement supports GeometryUtils, meaning it has getBoxQuads(), convertQuadFromNode(), convertRectFromNode(), convertPointFromNode().

Specific events are now also extended to have .pseudoTarget that is either CSSPseudoElement (if interaction has been with pseudo-element) or null. This allows to have more specific information on the event origin, e.g. that not just ultimate originating element (Event.target) has been clicked, but more specifically that it was ::after. Note that the Event.target is unchanged so event only has extra info on pseudo-element interaction.

The events are MouseEvent, PointerEvent, FocusEvent, AnimationEvent, TransitionEvent, KeyboardEvent, TouchEvent.
items.title: CSSPseudoElement interface

items.content_html:
The SVG specification allows the element to define its geometry using either an inline path attribute or a referenced path via href, with the path attribute taking precedence when both are specified.

While Safari/WebKit supports the path attribute on , the resolution behavior in certain cases is inconsistent or incomplete when compared to the specification and other engines. In particular, handling of precedence and fallback between path and href is not clearly defined or consistently applied, which can result in unexpected rendering differences.

This inconsistency creates interoperability issues for authors relying on spec‑compliant behavior and makes it difficult to author portable SVG text‑on‑path content without browser‑specific workarounds.

Expected behavior
SVG path resolution should follow the SVG specification:

  1. If both path and href are present, the inline path attribute should take precedence.
  2. If only path is present and valid, inline path data should be used.
  3. If path is invalid or missing, the implementation should fall back to resolving geometry from href.

Why this matters
Aligning WebKit behavior with the SVG specification improves interoperability across browser engines, reduces authoring complexity, and ensures predictable SVG text‑on‑path rendering across platforms.
items.title: Support path attribute on SVG <textpath> element

Description

This proposal adds an ai-disclosure global HTML attribute for declaring AI involvement at element-level granularity within a web page. It complements the page-level <meta> tag discussed in whatwg/html#9479 and the HTTP-level IETF AI-Disclosure header.

Four values aligned with the IETF header and IPTC Digital Source Type vocabulary: none, ai-assisted, ai-generated, autonomous.

<article>
  <section ai-disclosure="none">
    <p>Our investigation found...</p>
  </section>
  <aside ai-disclosure="ai-generated" ai-model="gpt-4o">
    <h3>AI Summary</h3>
    <p>The report concludes...</p>
  </aside>
</article>

Motivated by EU AI Act Article 50 (effective August 2026), which requires machine-readable marking of AI-generated text, and by 42+ comments on whatwg/html#9479 requesting element-level granularity that a page-level meta tag cannot provide.

According to the HTML specification, when a drag operation begins [1], the user agent should notify the drag source that the pointer event stream has ended and that no further events from this pointer should be expected [2]. Currently, no browsers fully implement this behavior. Chromium is moving forward to close this gap and align with the spec.

We’d appreciate your input on whether you have any concerns about making these events part of the web platform, or if the current lack of implementation is intentional.

[1] Drag and drop specifying that the pointer event should be suppressed on dragstart: Points (9) and (10)
[2] Pointer event spec definition of pointer stream suppression: https://w3c.github.io/pointerevents/#suppressing-a-pointer-event-stream

Preserving dropEffect Values from dragover to drop Events

WebKit Bugzilla URL

No response

Description

The HTML5 Drag and Drop API allows web applications to handle drag-and-drop operations through a series of events: dragstart, dragenter, dragover, dragleave, drop, and dragend. During these events, the dataTransfer.dropEffect property indicates which operation (copy, move, link, or none) should be performed. According to the HTML5 specification, the dropEffect value set by web applications during the last dragover event should be preserved and available in the subsequent drop event.

However, Chromium-based browsers/Webkit based browsers were overwriting the web application's dropEffect value with the browser's own negotiated operation before the drop event fired, breaking specification compliance and limiting developer control over drag-and-drop behavior.

Motivation

The current behavior:

  • Violates the HTML5 specification: Contradicts the standardized behavior defined in the HTML5 Drag and Drop API
  • Breaks developer control: Removes the ability for web applications to manage their own drag-and-drop operations
  • Creates unpredictable UX: The operation indicated during drag (via cursor feedback) may not match what's available in the drop handler
  • Forces workarounds: Developers must store dropEffect values in global variables or custom data attributes rather than using the standard API
  • Limits functionality: Makes it impossible to build spec-compliant file managers, code editors, and other applications requiring sophisticated drag-and-drop
items.title: Preserving dropEffect Values from dragover to drop Events

No response

WebKit Bugzilla URL

No response

Radar URL

Description

Requesting a position on a proposed, backwards-compatible addition to CSS Filter Effects to support progressive (gradient) blur — blur radius that varies spatially across an element (common for toolbar/footer scrims, bottom sheets, "fade-to-blur" overlays, tilt-shift effects).

CSSWG issue (full proposal + use cases + examples):
w3c/csswg-drafts#13285

Proposed API: linear-blur()

A new filter function modelled on linear-gradient() syntax:

filter: linear-blur([<angle> | to <side-or-corner>]?, <blur-stop-list>);
backdrop-filter: linear-blur([<angle> | to <side-or-corner>]?, <blur-stop-list>);

Where <blur-stop-list> follows the same pattern as gradient colour stops (blur value + optional position).

Examples:

/* Simple scrim */
.scrim {
  backdrop-filter: linear-blur(0px, 24px);
}

/* With stop positions */
.scrim {
  backdrop-filter: linear-blur(to bottom, 0px 0%, 0px 50%, 24px 100%);
}

/* Tilt-shift effect */
.tilt-shift {
  filter: linear-blur(to bottom, 8px, 0px 40%, 0px 60%, 8px);
}

Key semantics

This is spatially-varying blur, not blended output. The blur radius at each point is interpolated between stops — the convolution kernel size varies spatially. This is distinct from the existing workaround (backdrop-filter: blur() + mask-image) which blends between unblurred and uniformly-blurred output.

Implementation considerations: True spatially-varying blur is more expensive than uniform blur. Implementations may use approximations (mipmap-based, multi-pass, etc.) provided the visual result preserves detail in low-blur regions consistent with spatially-varying kernel sizes.

Why a new function?

  • Avoids overloading blur() parsing/semantics
  • Reuses the well-known gradient mental model
  • Creates a clear family for future variants (radial-blur(), conic-blur())

This is early-stage (no spec PR yet). Seeking implementer feedback on feasibility/performance and whether WebKit would be supportive/neutral/opposed to this direction.
items.title: Request for position: Progressive blur for Filter Effects: linear-blur()
